title: LEGO on Vinted: How to Buy Cheap Sets, Find Retiring Sets & Spot Fakes
intro: LEGO holds its value like almost nothing else in the toy aisle, and Vinted is one of the best places to buy it second-hand — complete sets, bulk lots and even retiring sets at well under retail. This guide covers how to find good LEGO on Vinted, how to spot fakes, and how to avoid the common pitfalls when buying bricks second-hand.

body.heading: Why LEGO is a great second-hand buy
paragraphs: LEGO is unusual among toys because it holds or even gains value. Complete sets — especially larger ones, licensed themes and sets that are retiring — often sell for close to or above their original retail price on the second-hand market. That makes it both a great thing to buy second-hand and a genuine collectible.

Vinted is a strong place to buy it because prices are often below eBay's, and the catalogue-style browsing makes it easy to search by theme and set number. Sellers are usually parents clearing out grown-up kids' bricks rather than dealers, which keeps prices realistic.
The catch is that LEGO second-hand has a few specific pitfalls — incomplete sets, missing minifigures, and counterfeit bricks — and a good buyer learns to check for all three before paying.

body.heading: How to find good LEGO on Vinted
paragraphs: Search by set number if you know it. Every LEGO set has a number (e.g. "75192" is the Millennium Falcon), and sellers who know what they have will put it in the title or description. Searching the number surfaces exactly that set and nothing else.

Search by theme if you don't — "LEGO Star Wars", "LEGO Harry Potter", "LEGO City" — then filter by price and condition. Bulk lots ("LEGO job lot", "LEGO bundle") are the cheapest way to buy by the kilogram, but they're a gamble on completeness, so know what you're buying.

Retiring sets are where the value is. Sets that LEGO is about to discontinue jump in price once they're gone from retail, so finding one second-hand just after retirement — or better, just before — is the sweet spot. Set an [alert for the sets you want](/guides/vinted-price-alert) so you catch them the moment they're listed, before another buyer does.

body.heading: How to spot fake LEGO
paragraphs: Counterfeit bricks (from brands like Lepin and other clone manufacturers) do appear on second-hand marketplaces, and the tell-tales are worth knowing. The most reliable check is the studs: genuine LEGO bricks have the word "LEGO" moulded into the top of every stud, while most fakes have blank or misspelled studs.

Check the minifigures carefully. Fake minifigures often have poor print quality, wrong colours, and misshapen hands or legs. On licensed themes like Star Wars or Harry Potter, the minifigures are often the most valuable part of the set, so they're the part most likely to be fake or swapped.

If a price seems too good for a large or retired set, treat it with extra caution and ask the seller for photos of the studs and the box. Genuine sellers selling a real set will happily send them; a seller who can't or won't is a red flag.
For broader safety when buying, read our [guide to Vinted scams and buyer protection](/guides/vinted-scams-buyer-protection).

body.heading: Check completeness before you pay
paragraphs: The single biggest risk buying LEGO second-hand is a set that's missing pieces. Always check the listing for whether the set is described as complete, and if it matters to you, ask the seller to confirm. 'Complete' means all pieces and minifigures; 'incomplete' means it's sold as-is.

For large sets, ask for the instruction booklet and check the piece count. A complete set will often still have its instructions, and many sellers state the piece count. If a set is missing instructions, the pieces may still be all there, but completeness is harder to verify.

Bulk lots sold by weight are priced for parts, not completeness — that's fine if you want a big pile of bricks to build with, but wrong if you're trying to assemble a specific set. Know which one you're buying.
If you're a seller rather than a buyer, 'complete' is the single most valuable word in your listing. A complete set with instructions sells for far more than the same bricks described vaguely.

body.heading: Buying and selling tips specific to LEGO
paragraphs: For buyers: minifigures drive value, so prioritise listings that clearly show them. Check the photos of the studs for the LEGO logo, ask about completeness, and be wary of anything too cheap for a retired or licensed set.

For sellers: list with the set number and theme in the title, state clearly whether it's complete, and photograph the studs and minifigures. Bundling a few smaller sets together often shifts them faster than listing each one alone.

Retiring and just-retired sets are the ones to watch — they're where the best deals are for buyers and the best margins are for resellers. [How to get more views on Vinted](/guides/how-to-get-more-views-on-vinted) applies here just as much as to clothes.

faq.question: Is LEGO cheaper on Vinted?
faq.answer: Often yes. Sellers on Vinted are usually parents clearing out bricks rather than dealers, so prices are frequently below eBay's. Searching by set number or theme and filtering by condition finds the best deals — especially for retiring or just-retired sets.

faq.question: How do I know if LEGO is fake on Vinted?
faq.answer: Check the studs: genuine LEGO has the word "LEGO" moulded into the top of every stud, while most fakes have blank or misspelled studs. Also check minifigure print quality and ask for photos of the studs and box if the price seems too good.

faq.question: What does 'complete' mean when buying LEGO second-hand?
faq.answer: It means the set includes all pieces and minifigures, and usually the instruction booklet. 'Incomplete' means it's sold as-is and may be missing pieces. Always confirm completeness if it matters, especially for large or valuable sets.

faq.question: Is LEGO a good thing to resell?
faq.answer: Yes, complete sets — especially licensed themes, large sets and retiring sets — hold or gain value. Minifigures drive the value. Buy retiring sets just after retirement and resell once retail stock is gone, and you can make a genuine margin.

faq.question: Are bulk LEGO lots worth buying?
faq.answer: For building, yes — bulk lots sold by weight are the cheapest way to get a big pile of bricks. For assembling a specific set, no — completeness isn't guaranteed, and missing pieces are the main risk. Know which one you're buying before you pay.
